newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seeks more transparent trading ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Spain seeks more transparent trading ahead of EMU.

text.p: The chairman of Spain's National Stock Market Commission (CNMV) promised on Wednesday to seek new, higher standards of transparency and responsibility in Spain's securities markets ahead of Europe's monetary union.
"European markets have to be more and more competitive," Juan Fernandez-Armesto told journalists at a presentation of the CNMV's annual report and its three-year strategic plan.
"We are trying to create a more serious and safer market...A well-regulated, serious market is the more attractive one."

The regulatory body plans to reduce transaction costs by trimming what it sees as excessive bureaucracy, while at the same time stepping up its watchdog role to encourage listed companies to be more forthright and honest with shareholders.
Foreign traders in Spain have long complained of the difficulty in wresting timely, relevant information from Spain's close-knit business community.
The business culture is a very personal one, with high value placed on friendships and contacts cemented over shared meals and drinks, workers for foreign companies in Madrid say.

Spanish traders move easily in this world, accepting that analysts at one brokerage may have access to some company news because of their special relationship with that company, but foreigners are troubled.
"That information is released depending on who is friends with whom is ridiculous," said one trader from a foreign bank, declining to be named.
Fernandez-Armesto said one of the major aims of his 26-point "A to Z" strategy was to make the Spanish trading climate more comfortable for all investors.

"Spanish companies have the habit of releasing loads of information on positive, but ultimately not relevant, issues," he said. "We want to step up demand for seriousness, transparency and responsibility."
He suggests asking companies to publish an annual information pamphlet written in "plain Spanish" with an analysis of the firm's situation and its markets.
The commission even plans to appoint an independent council to draw up a code of conduct for public quoted companies.
The code, which should be completed by October, will be voluntary, but firms will be obligated to report whether or not they abide by it.
The CNMV chairman believes there's room for improvement on the board of directors at Spanish firms as more and more big companies are privatised and placed on the stock exchange.
He would like to see more board members who are completely free of ties to the company, its suppliers or its subsidiaries to represent the interests of the minority stakeholders.
"The market is going to reward the companies that follow this code of conduct and punish those that do not," he said.
